s high levels, indicating PKU, physicians advise the parents to put the baby on a strict low-phenylalanine diet to protect the brain.","People need to avoid meats, eggs, dairy products, grains, and especially aspartame (NutraSweet), which is 50 percent phenylalanine.","Physicians formerly believed that children with PKU could quit the diet after a few years. Even a genetically normal baby cannot handle the enormous amounts of phenylalanine that an affected mother might pass through the placenta or milk.","A gene can influence brain development, but it can influence behavior even without being expressed in the brain.","If their reactions influence your personality, then your genes altered your behavior by altering your environment.","Now imagine a child born with genes promoting greater than average height and running speed. Because of these factors, the child shows early success at basketball, and soon spends more and more time playing basketball.","As a result, the child spends less time than average on other pursuits—watching videos, playing chess, or anything else.","The point is that genes can influence behavior in roundabout ways. We should not be surprised that nearly every human behavior has some heritability.","Evolution is a change over generations in the frequencies of various genes in a population.","For example, because humans are more similar to chimpanzees and bonobos than to other species, biologists infer a common ancestor.","As new evidence becomes available, biologists often change their opinions about the evolutionary relationship between one species and another.","In contrast, the question of how species do evolve is a question of how the process works, and that process is a necessary outcome from what we know about reproduction. Because plant and animal breeders have long understood this idea, they choose individuals with a desired trait and make them the parents of the next generation through a process called artificial selection.","If certain individuals are more successful than others in finding food, escaping enemies, resisting illness, attracting mates, or protecting their offspring, then their genes will become more prevalent in later generations.","Let’s clarify the principles of evolution by addressing a few misconceptions:","Natural selection cannot favor a gene that benefits the species while disadvantaging the individuals with the gene. Some people have claimed that when lemming populations become too high, some of the lemmings jump off cliffs to decrease the overpopulation problem.","If that were true (and it is not!), the next generation would all descend from lemmings that failed to jump.","It emphasizes evolutionary and functional explanations— that is, how our genes reflect those of our ancestors and why natural selection might have favored genes that promote certain behaviors.","The assumption is that any behavior characteristic of a species must have provided an advantage, at least in ancestral times.","For example, people get “goose bumps”—erections of the hairs, especially on their arms and shoulders—when they are cold or frightened. Goose bumps produce little if any benefit to humans because our shoulder and arm hairs are short and usually covered by clothing.","In most other mammals, however, erected hairs make a frightened animal look larger and more intimidating (Figure 4.6).","Here is another example of an evolutionary explanation, this time relating to old age: Throughout the animal kingdom, and for plants as well, life does not outlast the capacity to reproduce.","Living after you stop reproducing is disadvantageous from an evolutionary standpoint, because you would be competing with your offspring for food and shelter. Group selection works well for humans, because of our ability to punish or expel uncooperative people.","At its best, evolutionary psychology leads to research that helps us understand a behavior. The search for a functional explanation directs researchers to explore species’ different habitats and ways of life until we understand why they behave differently.","The approach is criticized when its practitioners propose speculative explanations without supporting evidence.","Many other behaviors are influenced by genes but also subject to strong influence by experience.","Our genes and our evolution make it possible for humans to be what we are today, but they also give us the flexibility to change our behavior as circumstances warrant.","Studying the genetics of behavior is more difficult with humans than with laboratory animals, because researchers have such limited control over environmental influences and no control over who mates with whom. Inferring how human behavior evolved is also difficult, because we do not know enough about the lives of our ancient ancestors.","Certain genes influence the probability of developing Alzheimer’s disease or other conditions that occur mostly in old Neurotrophins and cell death are part of this developmental process."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Experience continues to shape the developing nervous system. Follow the book’s discussion from early neural growth to adolescence and old age, keeping structural change and behavioral change related but distinct."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m4-2-study-1","text":"The developing nervous system"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Early development creates neurons and supporting cells, then organizes them into pathways. Neurons migrate toward appropriate destinations, axons grow toward targets, and synapses form. The mature architecture is not built by genes acting alone; activity, chemical cues, competition, and experience all help refine it. Axons respond to guidance signals, and neurons that fail to make suitable connections may undergo programmed cell death. Neurotrophins and other signals influence survival. Some new neurons can appear later in life, though this should not be confused with the brain routinely replacing every damaged neuron."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m4-2-study-2","text":"Competition and fine-tuning"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Developing circuits commonly create more contacts than are ultimately retained. Inputs compete, and patterns of activity help stabilize some synapses while others weaken or disappear. The cortex differentiates into functional regions over time; sensory and social experience can shape connectivity and dendritic structure. This is why timing matters: the same environmental event may have different effects at different developmental stages. Sensitive periods describe times when experience has unusually strong or lasting influence, not absolute one-time opportunities for all learning."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m4-2-study-3","text":"Development throughout life"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The developing brain is especially vulnerable to certain insults, including inadequate nutrition, toxic exposures, and injury. Adolescence involves continued changes in neural organization and behavioral regulation. Aging brings additional alterations in function and structure, but age-related change is variable and does not mean that plasticity disappears. A lifelong view avoids treating the adult brain as finished or treating every difference in the young brain as pathology."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m4-2-study-4","text":"What studies of experience can show"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Changes in synapses, dendrites, and cortical responses can follow training or altered input. Such changes demonstrate that experience is physically represented in the nervous system. Yet greater dendritic branching or a larger regional response is not automatically 'better'; interpretation depends on the behavior and circuit. The developmental story is one of guided growth followed by selective stabilization, change, and adaptation."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m4-2-h01","text":"Maturation of the Vertebrate A deficit in these chemicals leads to impaired migration, decreased brain size, and intellectual impairment.","The brain has many kinds of immunoglobulins and chemokines, reflecting the complexity of brain development.","Neurons develop different anatomies and functions, based on when and where they developed, and what genes they express.","Synaptogenesis, the formation of synapses, begins long before birth and continues throughout life, as neurons form new synapses and discard old ones. A slower stage of neuronal development is myelination, the process by which glia produce the insulating fatty sheaths that accelerate transmission in many vertebrate axons.","The traditional belief, dating back to Cajal’s work in the late 1800s, was that vertebrate brains formed all their neurons in embryological development or early infancy.","Beyond that point, neurons could modify their shape, but the brain could not develop new neurons.","However, researchers have discovered a few exceptions to the no-new-neurons rule.","In songbirds, one brain area that is necessary for singing loses neurons in fall and When researchers examined people’s skin cells, they found a concentration of 14 C corresponding to the year in which they did the test.","When researchers examined neurons in the cerebral cortex (of dead people at autopsy), they found a 14 C concentration corresponding to the year of the person’s birth.","These results indicate that the cerebral cortex forms no new neurons after the year of birth. In many mammals, new small interneurons form throughout life in the hippocampus, an important area for memory formation.","New neurons can be found in the human hippocampus up to about age 7, but beyond that age, some research methods have found evidence for new neurons and other methods have not.","If you asked someone to run a cable from one place to another in your room, your directions could be simple.","But imagine asking someone to run a cable to somewhere on the other side of the country. You would have to give detailed instructions about how to find the right city, the right building, and the location within the building.","The developing nervous system faces a similar challenge when it sends axons over great distances.","Biologist Paul Weiss conducted an experiment in which he grafted an extra leg to a salamander and then waited for axons to grow into it.","After the axons reached the muscles, the extra leg moved in synchrony with the normal leg next to it.","Today we compare the nervous system to computers, the most advanced technology of our era.) Later evidence supported the interpretation that Weiss had rejected: The salamander’s extra leg moved in synchrony with its neighbor because each axon found the correct muscle.","Roger Sperry, a former student of Weiss, performed a classic experiment that showed how sensory axons find their way to their correct targets. Sensory axons find their way in the same manner that axons to the muscles find their way.","Axons from other parts of the retina also grew back to their original targets.","Development proceeds by waves, as each type of neuron forms over a few days. Those that form earlier extend their axons longer and form more branches, thus making synapses with more targets.","Furthermore, neurons maturing at a particular time will make synapses with other neurons maturing at that time.","When axons reach their targets, chemical gradients steer them to approximately their correct location, but they cannot achieve perfect accuracy.","In fact, if a neuron cannot find its normal target (perhaps because that target has been damaged), in many cases it forms synapses onto some other target.","Each axon forms synapses onto many cells in approximately the correct location, and each target cell receives synapses from many axons. This adjustment depends on the pattern of input from incoming axons.","Consequently, axons from adjacent areas of the retina send almost simultaneous messages to the visual area of the thalamus.","In the development of the nervous system, we start with more neurons and synapses than we can keep, and then a selection process keeps the most successful combinations of synapses and rejects others. The principle of competition is an important one, although we should use the analogy with Darwinian evolution cautiously.","Each ganglion of the sympathetic nervous system has enough axons to supply all the muscles and glands in its area, with no axons left over.","Long ago, one hypothesis was that the muscles sent chemical messages to tell the sympathetic ganglion how many neurons to form.","She developed a love for research and eventually discovered that the muscles do not determine how many axons form. When any of its neurons forms a synapse onto a muscle, that muscle delivers a protein called nerve growth factor (NGF) that promotes the survival and growth of the axon.","It makes more neurons than necessary and discards the excess, thereby achieving a match between axons and targets.","In fact, all areas of the developing nervous system make more neurons than will survive into adulthood.","Nerve growth factor is a neurotrophin, meaning a chemical that promotes the survival and activity of neurons. (The word trophin derives from a Greek word for “nourishment.”) In addition to NGF, the nervous system responds to brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and several other neurotrophins. Recovery involves several possible processes, including relief from diaschisis, changes in axons, and adjustments in surviving networks."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The reorganized sensory representations associated with phantom limbs illustrate that experience depends on neural organization, not simply on current input. Distinguish biological recovery from learned behavioral compensation."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m4-3-study-1","text":"Immediate damage versus later consequences"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A brain injury can disrupt function directly through tissue damage and indirectly through swelling, inflammation, reduced blood flow, or changes in connected regions. Immediate treatment aims to limit further injury, while recovery over weeks and months involves different mechanisms. People can improve without returning to the exact pre-injury neural organization. It is therefore essential to distinguish anatomical repair from functional adaptation."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m4-3-study-2","text":"Several routes to recovery"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Diaschisis occurs when damage in one area depresses activity in connected regions; partial recovery may follow as those networks regain function. Surviving axons can sometimes sprout new branches, and other connections may strengthen. Denervation supersensitivity describes increased responsiveness after loss of normal input. True regrowth of long damaged axons in the adult central nervous system is limited, which helps explain why recovery is uneven. Training may support compensatory strategies even when lost tissue is not restored."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m4-3-study-3","text":"Cortical reorganization and phantom limbs"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Brain maps are not permanently fixed. When normal sensory input disappears, neighboring input can influence cortical regions that once responded to the missing body part. A person who has lost a limb may still experience sensations in it, including pain. Such phantom experiences show that body perception is generated by nervous-system representations rather than coming directly from current sensory input alone. Reorganization can be beneficial, but not every change automatically restores normal function."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m4-3-study-4","text":"Why rehabilitation is not a single technique"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Successful rehabilitation can involve physical practice, environmental supports, learning new routines, and addressing emotional or cognitive changes. The helpful intervention depends on the damage and the individual's remaining abilities. A sensible summary of plasticity is that neural circuits can adapt, but adaptation has biological constraints; clinical claims should be judged by controlled evidence and functional outcomes."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m4-3-h01","text":"Brain Damage and Immediate Treatments"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Possible causes of brain damage include tumors, infections, exposure
